name: E-democracy
summary: E-democracy (digital or internet democracy) holds that information and communication technology can deepen democratic life through online information, discussion, participation and sometimes direct or delegated voting. Its adherents mostly work within existing representative systems, aiming at more active citizen involvement, transparency and responsiveness, while treating security, privacy and the digital divide as serious risks. It is a procedural outlook and takes no side on most questions of economic or social policy.
scope: The mainstream civic-tech strand: Steven Clift's definition (coined 1994, Minnesota E-Democracy), participatory and deliberative platforms such as Decidim, and liquid-democracy tools like LiquidFeedback used by Pirate Parties. It excludes e-government service delivery as such and fringe technocratic or algorithmic-rule proposals. Most economic and social statements are answered neutral with low confidence because the ideology is procedural.

sources.usedFor: Definition: ICT used by democratic actors in political and governance processes at all levels, with greater and more direct citizen participation.

universal-healthcare.rationale: E-democracy is a method of political participation, not an economic program; adherents span the spectrum on health policy.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Nothing in e-democracy's doctrine addresses wage floors; it is a procedural stance and adherents differ.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The ideology is about civic technology and participation, not market versus state allocation, so adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: No source ties e-democracy to ownership of utilities; it is indifferent on the question.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Tax levels are not part of e-democracy's concerns; adherents hold varied views.

unions-good.rationale: Labor organization is outside the scope of e-democracy as documented; no position can be inferred.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property rights are not discussed in e-democracy sources; adherents are split.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation is not addressed by the ideology; its adherents are drawn from many economic camps.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare policy is outside e-democracy's procedural focus, so there is no inferable stance.

worker-ownership.rationale: Business ownership structures are not a theme of e-democracy; indifferent.

surveillance-ok.rationale: E-democracy sources list privacy and data security as key risks, and Decidim commits never to share personal data and to hide political preferences even from administrators, which sits uneasily with broad surveillance.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy is unrelated to e-democracy; adherents are split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Online deliberation advocates debate moderation, but the ideology takes no common line on legal speech limits.

strong-leader.rationale: E-democracy aims at more active citizen participation and revocable delegation, the opposite of a leader bypassing gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Its definition has governments and elected officials as legitimate democratic actors working with citizens; it seeks to improve governance, not abolish the state.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun policy has no connection to e-democracy; adherents are split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Security funding is not part of the ideology; no position inferred.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed by e-democracy; adherents hold varied views.

decide-locally.rationale: Clift's definition covers local, national and international levels, but the movement began with local and municipal forums, and tools like Decidim are widely used for city participation; mildly favours local decisions.

rehabilitation.rationale: Criminal justice philosophy is outside e-democracy's scope.

traditional-family.rationale: Family structure is not addressed; adherents are split.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Social-issue positions are not part of e-democracy; adherents vary.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; e-democracy is neutral on the substance of policy outcomes.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion's public role is outside e-democracy's concerns.

gender-social-construct.rationale: A theoretical question unrelated to civic technology; adherents split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cultural policy is not part of the ideology.

gradual-change.rationale: E-democracy proposals range from incremental add-ons to representative democracy to wholesale shifts toward direct models, so adherents are split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Clift's definition mentions the international level, but nothing shows the ideology wants international bodies empowered; adherents are split.

free-trade.rationale: Trade policy is outside e-democracy's scope.

nation-first.rationale: Not addressed; e-democracy tools are used both within and across nations.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign-policy questions are not part of e-democracy.

limit-growth.rationale: Environmental economics is not part of e-democracy.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Policy substance is left to participants; e-democracy takes no stance.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is unrelated to e-democracy.

revolution-justified.rationale: E-democracy works through existing democratic institutions and participation, so revolutionary change is not its method; inferred.

central-planning.rationale: Economic systems are not addressed by e-democracy.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land taxation is a fiscal-policy question that e-democracy sources never raise; adherents differ.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance tax is not a topic in e-democracy writing, and its adherents come from all fiscal camps.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade protection has no link to civic-technology doctrine; adherents are split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial policy is outside a movement about participation tools, so no stance exists.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Property distribution is not discussed in e-democracy sources.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; the ideology operates within existing political and economic systems, so a mild disagreement is inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions are not addressed in the e-democracy literature.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: E-democracy emphasizes open citizen participation over institutionalised interest bodies; inferred rather than stated.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The ideology is defined as democratic actors using ICT in governance; hereditary rule has no place in it.

democracy-best.rationale: E-democracy is by definition an effort to strengthen democracy, though sources do not address the case of voters choosing badly.

direct-votes.rationale: Clift's definition notes many see e-democracy as enabling more direct citizen involvement, and liquid democracy lets voters vote on any policy directly; yet the field also works within representative systems, so +1.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils as basis of power are not an e-democracy topic; adherents split.

right-to-secede.rationale: Secession is a territorial question the ideology does not take up; online referendums could serve either side.

war-builds-character.rationale: Inferred from the participatory, civic-minded orientation; not addressed.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Equality of participation and access in Decidim's contract rules this out.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Decidim's contract calls equality in political participation a fundamental principle and gives every user an equal starting point.

socialism-one-country.rationale: An internal Marxist debate that e-democracy sources do not touch.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The colonial framing of settler states is not addressed by e-democracy writing.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Personal law is not an e-democracy topic.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Open access and privacy principles suggest opposition; the issue is not addressed.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious-cultural policy not addressed by e-democracy sources.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: School religion policy is not discussed in e-democracy writing.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Participatory, transparent governance sits poorly with a strengthened state apparatus; inferred.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Its aim is more active citizen participation and responsiveness in governance, rooting authority in citizens' involvement.

trade-surplus.rationale: Trade balance policy is outside e-democracy's scope.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced removal of a minority contradicts equal participation and universal access in Decidim's contract.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; adherents hold varied ethical views.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Not addressed; adherents split between open participation and protecting democratic order.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Philosophical conception of freedom not addressed.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Not addressed, though bridging the digital divide is a concern.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law is not part of e-democracy doctrine.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: A Malthusian claim that e-democracy sources never discuss.

notes: E-democracy is a procedural family, so most substantive policy answers are neutral and low confidence and will not count as stated positions. Strands differ: liquid democracy leans to direct and delegated voting, while others only add consultation to representative institutions.
